To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
for a DEIF of 55 m (e.g. for large trees), 9 of the 31 studied forest islands still contain a core area of more than 40%.

for a DEIs of 55 m, which is a DEI that is often used for forest island analyses, only 9 of 31 studied forest islands in the Comoe National Park, Ivory Coast, have an rCA of more than 0.50, and that this rCA increases exponentially with increasing DEIs.

(1) the core area of the studied forest fragments is highly dependent on the DEI, (2) the core area is not a constant value, but varies from 5% to 100% of the total forest island area, (3) the rCA of the studied forest island was 50% for a DEI between 40 and 60 m, and (4) the rCA increased exponentially with increasing values for DEI.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how to define a minimum size of forest islands that can still be considered as a habitat for forest-interior species, and we conclude that a size of 40 ha should be a minimum for a forest island to still contain a core area that is large enough to harbour forest-interior species.
the question of how large forest islands need to be to protect forest interior species, and how large the core-area is in which these species can be protected.
the question of how much area is necessary to protect biodiversity in a forest-savanna mosaic, and how much of that area can be considered core area.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
forest islands in the study area are not large enough to guarantee a core area of more than 10–20% for large forest tree species.

the protection of forest interior species in natural forest islands and forest fragments requires the preservation of large forest islands with a minimum size of 36 ha, but also that smaller islands can be considered as important for the protection of species with a lower habitat specificity, or if they are located in a mosaic of forest islands and forest patches.
forest islands in the studied area are too small for most forest interior species to survive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
forest islands of a size of at least 36 ha are required to maintain a forest interior species composition.
in the Comoé Park, forest islands of 36.7 ha or more should be protected in order to guarantee the existence of a forest-core area for the majority of forest-interior tree species.
the protection of forest interior species is only possible for a small number of forest islands in the study area.
The main takeaway from our work is that
core-area analysis is an essential part of any forest island study and that core-area size should be considered as a critical factor for the protection of biodiversity.
the protection of forest species is not necessarily linked to the protection of the whole forest area, but rather to the protection of core areas.
the size of forest islands is of crucial relevance for their protection and management.
